# Šāpšu walks into a solar & renewable energy firm

Walk into any solar & renewable energy outfit and watch for ten minutes. You will see a very old act performed with newer props. The act has a name. It is **Šāpšu**.

## Before the Office, the Story

**The Lamp of the Gods.** No long narrative myth of Šāpšu survives; her personality must be gathered from epithets scattered across the tablets, and the most telling is nrt ʾilm špš — 'the Lamp of the Gods, Shapash' (KTU 1. 16 i and parallels).  The image is domestic and cosmic at once: the sun is the oil lamp of the divine household, lit each morning so that the gods can see their own world.

**Finding Baꜥal in the Dark.** When Baꜥal dies, the storm's sisters are helpless until the one goddess who can see in every direction is enlisted.  In KTU 1. 6 iv, ꜥAnat raises her voice to the sun goddess and begs Šāpšu to search for Baꜥal through the day and through the underworld itself.

## The Reveal, Seat by Seat

### Solar & Renewable Energy

*Ugarit’s sun-goddess, the torch that crosses the sky by day and descends to the dead at evening — the Levant’s solar deity.* The match is not poetic license. Strip the trade to its function and the function is the myth.

### Legal, Justice & Compliance

*The divine witness whose light exposes every scheme; justice as illumination.* The match is not poetic license. Strip the trade to its function and the function is the myth.

### Optics, Imaging & Vision

*The torch of the gods whose rays penetrate every hidden corner; the all-seeing eye of the Ugaritic pantheon.* Nobody in that trade worships at this temple. They just keep its hours.

### Communication, Messaging & Logistics

*The gods’ messenger, carrying the word between heaven, earth, and the underworld.* Nobody in that trade worships at this temple. They just keep its hours.

## Not the First Rebrand

Šāpšu's nearest relative is the Mesopotamian sun god Shamash — another all-seeing luminary who patrols heaven and underworld and stands witness to oaths — though Šāpšu is a goddess where Shamash is a god, one of the few female solar deities of the ancient Near East.  The winged sun disk that spreads over Phoenician, Aramaean, and Israelite royal iconography carries the protective radiance of the same solar court. The office is only the latest translation.
